title: Trained on 2019
concept: A study in Earth's Future (November 24th) by Andreas Krause's team at the Technical University of Munich trained an XGBoost machine learning model on lightning and weather observations from one year, 2019, six everyday weather readings and where ground strikes landed on a half-degree grid. On today's climate most of Alaska got under one strike per square kilometer a year. By 2100 under high emissions Alaska could get 116 to 594 percent more, the world's land 76 to 140 percent. Lightning fires burned at least 93 percent of Alaska's wildfire acres every year for a decade, but the study didn't model fire. Krause was quite surprised the projections were so high. Run backward the model estimated about 12 percent more lightning per degree; earlier studies projected 8 to 17; run forward its own 12 could nearly triple to 30, and the release says earlier studies differ mostly in math. The twist: a month earlier Krause and Anja Rammig posted a preprint in which a simple average beat the machine learning lightning models it tested, and advised testing models outside their training conditions. In fairness the paper's model beat a regression and three existing formulas. Read it as a range that waits on that test. Drawn as a teardrop glass instrument labelled THE MODEL with a wax seal stamped 2019, a hatched lemon range column beside a paper TODAY token, a dial whose two gear trains differ, a sleepy ruler that wins a race the model isn't in, and an envelope addressed ML LIGHTNING MODELS whose card ends on a stake beside the still-sealed glass.

divergence_note: Against the last four films: 11-26 celadon CT tile and graphite under a bone lightbox key with an orchid #D94FB0 pulse (hue about 318), indoors before dawn; 11-25 bone noon snow at a rail fork with railway amber #F2A93B (about 38); 11-24 flat July overcast on olive tundra with vermilion pins (about 8); 11-23 apricot-plum civil twilight on river ice with scarlet (about 355). This film is outdoors under a green-slate storm sky (#2F3A3A, about 180) with a golden ember band, and its only saturated accent is lemon #FFE45C (about 52) for lightning alone; the hero glass is smoke-lilac #DCD6E6 (about 260), far from 11-26's celadon; fireweed is muted buds only. The hero is a teardrop glass instrument sealed with wax in a brass bracket, which differs from 11-23's SampleTube (a stoppered upright cylinder in a lab rack) by silhouette (teardrop vs cylinder), closure (wax-sealed neck vs stopper) and mount (field bracket vs rack), and it performs mostly through its physics, not a face's moods. Honest overlaps: a true Alaska map seen from above in one shot (S16; S5 is a low oblique), a brass needle dial (11-24 used gauges), a race gag (11-26 had a printer losing to a phone), and conifers from the shelf.

treatment.title: Trained on 2019
treatment.summary: Winner B (the Dramatist) with grafts from the Explainer (a paper TODAY token and a hatched lemon range band, the sensitivity dial against an EARLIER STUDIES band), the Comedian (the AVERAGE ruler that lies there and wins, a raven that ducks the bolts) and the Enthusiast (the June 23rd, 2024 storm day on the map). Hero recast from a faced fork tree (11-16's VoteTree idiom) to a teardrop glass instrument labelled THE MODEL.
treatment.judge_reasoning: Judge reasoning: the Dramatist's spine is the only one whose picture IS the argument: the model is sealed with its training year, and THE TEST is an envelope addressed ML LIGHTNING MODELS whose card ends on a stake beside the still-sealed glass, planted at about 20 s and opened at 98 s. Both the Dramatist and the Enthusiast cast a faced tree of yes/no forks (Sprig), which repeats 11-16's VoteTree idiom, so the hero is recast as a TEARDROP GLASS INSTRUMENT with a wax-sealed neck in a brass bracket, eyes in a dark lens, crystals growing from its bottom, labelled THE MODEL (the words storm glass never appear on screen, since storm glasses have no forecasting skill). Gate 0 rounds moved the picture to the record: one hatched treatment for the whole projected range (TODAY is the only solid token), no damage or verdict on the seal, the preprint never touching the model except by a cord marked OUR READ, and 'different math' drawn as two gear trains.

angle.thesis: A machine learning model that learned from 2019's lightning says Alaska could get more than double, up to nearly seven times, today's ground strikes under high emissions, and the honest read is a range: even its floor matters in a state where lightning fires burn nearly all the acres, while its ceiling is the question its own authors taught us to ask, will it hold outside the conditions it trained on.
angle.falsifiability: False if a test outside the training conditions (the test the authors' preprint calls for, c21) shows this model does no better than a simple training-average benchmark (what the preprint found for the ML models it tested, c20), because then even the floor would carry no skill. Also false in its first half if the floor were not more than double (c8 says +116%), or if lightning were a minor cause of Alaska's burned acres (c23 says at least 93% every year 2015 to 2024).
supporting_facts: The mechanism: an XGBoost model trained on lightning and weather observations from 2019 (c3, c4), six everyday weather readings (c5), ground strikes on a half-degree grid (c6). Run on today's climate most of Alaska got under one bolt per sq km a year (c7).

The number is a range: Alaska +116% to +594% under high emissions, per AGU (c8), the top nearly sevenfold (c9), against the world's +76% to +140% (c10). The Alaska range is much wider than the world's (our arithmetic on c8 and c10, never the study's claim, never explained).

The stakes are Alaska's: lightning fires burned at least 93% of wildfire acres every year 2015 to 2024 (c23), about 3.1 million acres in 2022 (c24). The study didn't model fire (c25), so fire is context, kept apart from the projection.
angle.counterpoint_to_honor: Two fair cases, each a scene. The method question at full strength: the model learned from one year (c3); run backward it gives about 12% per degree (c11, c12), inside earlier studies' 8 to 17% (c14), but forward it gives about 30% (c13), and the release says the gap is mostly different math (c14); Krause was 'quite surprised' (c15) and names 'quite a large uncertainty' (c16); a month earlier Krause and Rammig's preprint found a simple training-average benchmark beat the ML lightning models it tested and warned scores can overstate projection skill (c19, c20, c21). Never said to have tested this model, never says the sensitivity causes the width. The model's defense, shown straight: it beat a regression and three existing formulas (c22), and separate work already found boreal lightning ignitions rising since 1975 (c27).
angle.valence_defense: ML does real work here and points at the thing that lights nearly all of Alaska's fires, so doom is wrong and dismissal is wrong. It's an unvalidated high-emissions projection whose authors flag their own field's evaluation limits, so celebration would oversell it. The film shows what the range is made of and lets the floor land.
angle.who_it_serves: Alaskans who live with lightning-fire summers, Alaska fire and land managers, the legislators who fund suppression, and Alaska researchers placed to run the outside-the-training-data test.
angle.second_movement: The recontextualising fact is the October 17th preprint by two of the same authors: test scores can overstate projection skill, test models outside their training conditions. It turns the film from 'a scary number' into 'a number that comes with its own test', and the button asks who should run that test.

runner_ups.angle: Analyst A: Alaska gets a gridded projection of its main fire igniter and should use the range as a planning envelope
runner_ups.why_lost: 'never had' is unsupported (earlier projections exist, r1), and 'planning envelope' skips the preprint's warning; kept as the closing question.

runner_ups.angle: Analyst B: the stretch of the range rides a sensitivity jump from 12 to 30 percent per degree
runner_ups.why_lost: no claim says the sensitivity causes the range's width, and it left out the Alaska fire stakes; kept as the Act 3 methods scene.

runner_ups.angle: Analyst C: the width is the finding, treat 'more than double' as the floor and 'nearly 7x' as an open question
runner_ups.why_lost: the core survived as the synthesis, but 'rests on a sensitivity' was an unsupported causal link and the range must always be given whole.

constraints_carried: per AGU and PROJECTION on every Alaska figure
the whole range, could, high emissions
fire is Division of Forestry context, the study didn't model fire
the preprint is about ML lightning models in general, never this model
the Amazon caveat is never applied to Alaska
never say the sensitivity explains the width
Krause and Rammig by surname, never gendered
observations from 2019, never one storm season
